passage: Zeenat, you asked why old Sudha Aunty still keeps a notebook of questions. Let me tell you. The winter I was ten, fog sat on our village for weeks, and I noticed the dew on the spider webs vanished by noon but stayed in the shade of the well. Nobody at school taught that. So every morning I checked three webs, one sunny, one shady, one near the stove smoke, and wrote down when the drops went. My brother Kishan called me mad. Then the science master saw my notebook and lent me his own book on weather. I read it under the quilt by lantern light. That notebook was the first of forty.

qa.q: How many webs did Sudha check every morning?
qa.a: She checked three webs, one sunny, one shady, one near the stove smoke.

qa.q: Why did young Sudha keep checking the webs every morning?
qa.a: She was curious and fascinated by why the dew lasted longer in the shade, and wanted to find out for herself.

qa.q: What turning point came when the science master saw Sudha's notebook?
qa.a: By lending her his own book on weather, he encouraged her to keep investigating, and that notebook became the first of forty.

qa.q: How did Kishan see his sister's web-checking?
qa.a: Kishan thought it was mad, probably not understanding why anyone would study dew without being told to.

grounding: Shows a child's own drive to investigate a question about dew beyond anything taught at school, told as an elder's memory.

passage:
Dear Diary, 14 April, Baisakhi holiday
Today the colony kids split up for real. Tanmay's lot say only people who can bowl fast are in the "Tigers". Urmila and I aren't fast, so we sat on the water tank and started our own group: the Comic Keepers. Rules: you must own at least one comic, you must bring snacks on Sundays, and no Tigers allowed. Urmila drew a badge. Ravi wanted to join, but he doesn't have any comics, so I said no. He walked off kicking stones. I felt a bit bad, but rules are rules. Tomorrow we meet at five.
Mohit

qa.q: What is the name of the group Mohit and Urmila started?
qa.a: The Comic Keepers.

qa.q: How did Mohit feel after saying no to Ravi?
qa.a: Mohit felt a bit bad and uneasy, but held on to the idea that rules are rules.

qa.q: What could Mohit and Urmila do so their club doesn't shut people out the way the Tigers did?
qa.a: They could relax the comic rule, for example lending Ravi one, so the club is about a shared interest rather than keeping people out.

qa.q: What is it like for Ravi to be turned away?
qa.a: Ravi feels rejected and hurt, kicking stones on the way out, much as Mohit and Urmila were shut out by the Tigers.

grounding: Illustrates children forming a club with shared interests and firm rules about who is in and who is out.

passage: Beta, you want to know about my oldest friend? I'm your Vandana Nani, and at ten I thought friends were just whoever sat beside me. Then, the monsoon I turned eleven, Gurleen moved into our lane. One wet afternoon under the neem tree, she told me she couldn't swim and was terrified of the school picnic at the river. She made me pinky-swear not to tell. At the picnic the other girls splashed and shouted, "Come in!" I said, "Gurleen's helping me collect shells," and we walked the bank together. She squeezed my hand. Sixty years later, she still calls me every monsoon.

qa.q: What did Gurleen tell Vandana under the neem tree?
qa.a: She told her she couldn't swim and was terrified of the school picnic at the river.

qa.q: What did young Vandana want when she said Gurleen was helping her collect shells?
qa.a: She wanted to spare Gurleen embarrassment, feeling loyal and protective of her friend's secret.

qa.q: Which choice at the picnic mattered most, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the promise and giving Gurleen a reason to stay on the bank protected her secret, and turned a new neighbour into a lifelong friend.

qa.q: What was the picnic like for Gurleen?
qa.a: Gurleen was scared of the water and the girls' shouting, so Vandana's help probably brought her huge relief.

grounding: Shows a child's friendship deepening into loyalty when she keeps a friend's secret, told as a grandmother's memory.

passage: Leela, your Usha Ammamma was twelve once too, you know. The Onam before I moved to the town school, I wore my old green frock to the class celebration. Every other girl wore a cream-and-gold pavada, with jasmine in her plait. Nobody said a word, but they stood a little apart from me in the photo. That evening I thought about how they walked, how they folded their hands, who sat where. I asked Amma to alter my cousin's old pavada. On the last day before the holidays I wore it, with jasmine, and Beena waved me into the middle of the line. I felt warm and a little strange, as if I'd learned a password.

qa.q: What did every other girl wear to the class celebration?
qa.a: A cream-and-gold pavada, with jasmine in her plait.

qa.q: How did young Usha feel when the girls stood apart in the photo?
qa.a: She felt left out and self-conscious, noticing an unspoken rule she hadn't known about.

qa.q: What turning point came that evening, and what did it lead to?
qa.a: Usha chose to study the girls' unspoken habits and ask Amma to alter the pavada, which got her waved into the middle of the line.

qa.q: How might Beena have seen Usha on the last day?
qa.a: Beena seems to see Usha as one of the group now, welcoming her into the middle of the line.

grounding: Illustrates a child noticing and then following unspoken rules about festival dress, told as a grandmother's memory.

passage: The first real snow had fallen in Tromsø, and the slope behind the school was packed at break. Anders, the biggest boy in fifth grade, had taken the best sledge and was deciding who got a go. "Not you, Emil. You're too slow." Emil's face went hot. He almost ran to the teacher on duty, then stopped. Instead he gathered the others. "Let's go in order of who got here first. Everyone gets two runs." Most of them nodded. Anders scowled, outnumbered. "Fine. But I go first." "You were first anyway," Emil said. By the bell, Anders was pushing the little ones off from the top himself.

qa.q: How many runs did Emil suggest each person get?
qa.a: Everyone gets two runs.

qa.q: Why did Emil stop himself from running to the teacher on duty?
qa.a: He felt hurt and angry, but seemed confident the group could agree on a fair rule without help.

qa.q: What made Emil's plan work?
qa.a: He offered a simple, fair rule and got the others to agree first, so Anders couldn't just overrule him. 👍

qa.q: What is it like for Anders when the others nod at Emil's plan?
qa.a: Anders feels outnumbered and a bit put out, but accepts because Emil lets him save face by going first.

grounding: Shows children settling a power struggle over a sledge among themselves instead of calling an adult.

passage:
"Sudha, you're not playing Holi with us?" Saurabh asked. She stood by the school gate, arms folded, eyes on her shoes.
"I just don't feel like it."
Saurabh started, "Come on, it's fun, you'll..." then stopped. Her shoulders were up near her ears. He waited.
"My new kurta," she said finally. "Ma saved up for it. If it gets coloured..."
"Oh." He nodded. "So you do want to play, just not in that."
"Yes!"
"I've got an old T-shirt in my bag. It's huge on me."
Sudha looked up for the first time. "Really?"
"Really."

qa.q: What did Sudha not want to get coloured?
qa.a: Her new kurta.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh stop mid-sentence and wait?
qa.a: He noticed Sudha's raised shoulders and felt concerned that something was wrong, so he chose to listen instead of pushing.

qa.q: What could Saurabh try next time a friend goes quiet?
qa.a: He could do the same again: notice body cues, stop talking, and give the friend time to explain.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel when Saurabh offers his T-shirt?
qa.a: Sudha feels relieved and understood, because Saurabh heard the real reason instead of just urging her to play. 😊

grounding: Illustrates a child reading a friend's body language during Holi and listening without interrupting.

passage:
Dear Diary, 2 May, summer holidays
It was so hot today that Mummy made mango panna. She poured one full steel tumbler for me and one for Sunaina. Then Sunaina tipped hers into the tall thin glass and shouted, "Now I have more!" Mummy laughed and asked me. I looked hard. The tall glass looked fuller, but I poured it back into the tumbler and it filled it exactly, not a drop more. "Same amount, it just changed shape," I said. Sunaina sulked and said I was cheating. Tomorrow I'll show her with water and the measuring jug.
Gargi

qa.q: What did Mummy make because it was so hot?
qa.a: She made mango panna.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel after pouring the panna back into the tumbler?
qa.a: Gargi felt sure and satisfied, having proved that the amount stayed the same. 😊

qa.q: How could Gargi help Sunaina see the idea tomorrow?
qa.a: Gargi could let Sunaina do the pouring with water and the measuring jug, so Sunaina sees the level match.

qa.q: Why might Sunaina think the tall glass has more?
qa.a: Sunaina judges by how high the drink reaches, so the tall thin glass looks fuller, and being told otherwise feels like cheating.

grounding: Shows a child understanding that the amount of a drink stays the same when it is poured into a differently shaped glass.

passage:
Tutor's note, Shimla, 20 January
It was so cold this week that a bowl of water on the school steps froze overnight. Nitin brought it in and watched it melt by the heater. "It can go back to ice if we put it out tonight," he said. Later we did sums. He wrote 8 + 6 = 14, and I asked what 14 − 6 would be. He stared, then grinned. "Eight! You just undo it, like the ice." He tried three more on his own. His friend Aman said, "That's a trick!" Nitin explained it to him. I've asked his mother to try "undo" questions at home.
Sangeeta Ma'am

qa.q: What sum did Nitin write?
qa.a: He wrote 8 + 6 = 14.

qa.q: What does Nitin's grin after answering "Eight!" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt excited and proud at discovering that a sum can be undone, just like the ice.

qa.q: What else could Nitin's mother ask to build on this?
qa.a: She could ask "undo" questions like "If I add 3 and then take away 3, where are we?", or let him fold and unfold paper.

qa.q: How does Aman react to Nitin's discovery?
qa.a: Aman thinks it's a trick at first, then gets to hear Nitin explain it.

grounding: Illustrates a child realising that melting ice and an addition sum can both be reversed back to where they started.

passage: It was harvest time in their village near Hoshangabad, and Dadaji's small grain shop was piled with sacks. Seema and her cousin Ritu were told to label the tins. Ritu wrote "rice", "wheat", "moong", "masoor" and "chana" and lined them up in a row. Seema frowned. "Rice and wheat are grains. Moong, masoor and chana are dals. And all of them are food we sell." On the slate she drew a big circle marked FOOD, and inside it two smaller circles, GRAINS and DALS. Dadaji peered over his glasses. "And where do moong sprouts go?" Seema thought. "Inside dals, in a smaller circle." Ritu clapped.

qa.q: What did Seema write in the big circle on the slate?
qa.a: She marked the big circle FOOD.

qa.q: Why did Seema frown at Ritu's row of labels?
qa.a: She was dissatisfied because the row didn't show how the items belonged together, and she wanted a clearer order.

qa.q: How could Dadaji use Seema's circles in the shop?
qa.a: He could arrange the shelves by the same groups, grains on one side and dals on the other, so customers find things quickly.

qa.q: What is it like for Ritu to see Seema's circles?
qa.a: Ritu is impressed and delighted, clapping when Seema fits the sprouts into a smaller circle.

grounding: Shows a child organising shop goods into groups within groups during harvest time.

passage: Zeenat, you asked why an old accountant like Arnab keeps watercolours in his desk drawer. When I was eleven, the winter fog in our Bardhaman town lay on the pond every morning. One day my uncle, who painted signboards, woke me at dawn. "Look," he said. The fog was pink where the sun touched it, and a heron stood in it like a pencil line. I didn't speak. He gave me his oldest brush and a scrap of card, and I tried to paint it. It was a mess, all brown. But I went back every foggy morning that winter. My mother pinned the seventh painting above the stove. I still paint the fog, badly, every December.

qa.q: What stood in the fog like a pencil line?
qa.a: A heron stood in it like a pencil line.

qa.q: What was young Arnab feeling when he stood silent at the pond?
qa.a: He felt awed and moved by the pink fog and the heron, too struck by the beauty to speak.

qa.q: What turning point came when the uncle handed Arnab a brush?
qa.a: Being given a brush turned quiet looking into trying, and Arnab kept painting every foggy morning, a habit that lasted a lifetime.

qa.q: How might Arnab's mother have felt pinning up the seventh painting?
qa.a: She probably felt proud and touched, seeing her son's steady effort and wanting to celebrate it.

grounding: Illustrates a child's growing sensitivity to natural beauty and first attempts to paint it, told by a senior colleague.
